# 1: Project Overview

With grocery prices continuing to rise across Canada and the world affording basic necessities has become an increasing challenge for many households. According to Statistics Canada, approximately **9.8 million Canadians (24% of the population)** experienced some form of food insecurity in 2024. In this project, I will analyze grocery prices and minimum wages across all 10 Canadian provinces over the past decade (2016–2026) to estimate how many hours a person earning minimum wage would need to work to be able to afford a basic basket of groceries. I will be focusing on how affordability has changed since the COVID 19 and whether minimum wages have kept up with the rising cost of food.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 2: Data Sources

## 2.1 Summary of sources

For this project, I identified two main data sources that will help me investigate grocery affordability across Canada. The first is Statistics Canada's monthly average retail food prices dataset, which provides grocery price information across provinces. The second is the Government of Canada's historical minimum wage dataset, which provides minimum hourly wage rates across provinces over time. I will combine these datasets to compare the cost of basic groceries with minimum wages and calculate how much time someone earning minimum wage would need to work to afford them over the years. I will also look at how this has changed since COVID19.

```{r source-summary, echo=FALSE}
sources <- tribble(
  ~Source,            ~Producer,          ~Format,  ~Coverage,          ~Using,
  "Monthly Average Retail Prices for Selected Products: Food",    "Statistics Canada",   "CSV",  "Canada; past decade data",   "Yes",
  "Historical Minimum Wage Rates in Canada",    "Employment and Social Development Canada",   "CSV",  "Canada in past decade",   "Yes",
)

knitr::kable(sources)
```

## 2.2.1: Monthly Average Retail Prices for Selected Products: Food

Source:https://www150.statcan.gc.ca/t1/tbl1/en/tv.action?pid=1810024502

**Producer and authority.** This dataset is published by Statistics Canada, Canada's national statistical agency. Statistics Canada collects and publishes economic and social data to help Canadians understand changes in the country's economy and population. The dataset is part of its consumer price and food price stats.

**Original Dataset Purpose.** The original purpose of this dataset was to provide information about average prices for commonly purchased food products across Canada. It allows people to examine food prices across different provinces and time. Although it wasn't specifically created to measure affordability for minimum-wage workers it provides the grocery price information i needed for my project.

**Collection method.** According to Statistics Canada's documentation, average retail food prices are calculated using transaction data obtained directly from Canadian grocery retailers. This information comes from retailers' systems and includes details about products, quantities sold, and transaction prices.

**Coverage and resolution.** The dataset covers Canada, individual provinces and territories, and selected population centres. It is updated monthly and reports average retail prices for different food products in Canadian dollars. For my project, I will focus on the ten Canadian provinces and investigate the historical data available for the past decade (2016–2026). I will use the monthly prices to calculate annual averages where appropriate.

**Licence.** Open Government Licence – Canada. The dataset is available for public use, subject to the terms of the licence

**Access.** I accessed the dataset through the Statistics Canada website using Table 18-10-0245-02. The data can be downloaded in CSV format directly from the website. I accessed the source on November 5th 2026.

**Known problems.** One limitation is that the products and their categories may change over time, which can make direct price comparisons difficult. Statistics Canada also notes that the composition of product categories can change because of differences in consumer preferences, product availability, quality, and quantity. In addition, the retailer data coverage was expanded in January 2024, which may affect comparisons between earlier and later years. Some products may also have missing prices for certain provinces or months.

```{r source-1-load}

library(tidyverse)

raw_alberta <- read_csv("data/raw/Alberta.csv", skip = 9)
raw_bc <- read_csv("data/raw/British Columbia.csv", skip = 9)
raw_manitoba <- read_csv("data/raw/Manitoba.csv", skip = 9)
raw_nb <- read_csv("data/raw/New Brunswick.csv", skip = 9)
raw_nl <- read_csv("data/raw/Newfoundland and Labrador.csv", skip = 9)
raw_ns <- read_csv("data/raw/Nova Scotia.csv", skip = 9)
raw_ontario <- read_csv("data/raw/Ontario.csv", skip = 9)
raw_pei <- read_csv("data/raw/PEI.csv", skip = 9)
raw_quebec <- read_csv("data/raw/Quebec.csv", skip = 9)
raw_saskatchewan <- read_csv("data/raw/Saskatchewan.csv", skip = 9)

glimpse(raw_alberta)
```

The output shows that the Alberta dataset contains 115 rows and 86 columns. It includes grocery products in the first column and monthly average retail prices in the remaining columns, covering September 2019 to September 2026. The prices are recorded in dollars and the dataset includes information for different grocery items across each month. One thing I noticed is that the first row contains the unit of measurement ("Dollars") rather than an actual grocery product.

## 2.2.2 Historical Minimum Wage Rates in Canada

Source: <https://open.canada.ca/data/en/dataset/390ee890-59bb-4f34-a37c-9732781ef8a0>

**Producer and authority.** This dataset is published by Employment and Social Development Canada. The department publishes historical minimum wage information as part of its labour market and employment related statistics.

**Original Dataset Purpose.** The purpose of this dataset is to provide historical information about minimum wage rates in Canada. The dataset makes it possible to examine how minimum wages have changed over time. For my project, I will use these rates to compare wage increases with changes in grocery prices.

**Collection method.** The dataset provides historical minimum wage rates. However, the dataset description does not clearly explain the original collection process or how the historical rates were verified.

**Coverage and resolution.** The dataset covers Canadian provinces and territories. The information is organized by geographic area and applicable wage rate. Unlike the grocery price dataset, which is updated monthly, minimum wage rates change when new wage adjustments come into effect. For my analysis, I will use the rates applicable during each year from 2016 to 2026 and account for changes that occurred within a year.

**Licence.** Open Government Licence – Canada. The dataset is publicly available and can be downloaded in CSV format

**Access.** I accessed this dataset through the Government of Canada's Open Government Portal. It provides downloadable CSV files in English and French. Other researchers can access the same dataset through the portal. I accessed the source on November 5th 2026.

**Known problems.** One challenge is that minimum wage rates change at different times and frequencies across provinces. I must use the exact rate for each specific period rather than assuming it stays the same all year.

```{r source-2-load}

library(tidyverse)

raw_wages <- read_csv("data/raw/wages_general-2.csv")

glimpse(raw_wages)
```

The dataset contains 597 rows and 4 columns, including jurisdiction, effective date, minimum wage, and additional notes. The wage values are stored as character data because they include dollar signs, so I will need to convert them to numeric values before analysis.

## 2.3: Investigated and rejected sources

So far, I have not selected any alternative datasets to reject. My research has mainly focused on finding grocery price and minimum wage data that cover all Canadian provinces.

## 2.4: What I could not find

I could not find one dataset that directly compares grocery prices with minimum wages across Canada. Instead, I found two separate datasets that I will combine for my analysis.

I also found that the grocery price data only goes back to September 2019 for some provinces, rather than covering the full ten years I originally planned.

## 3.3: Downstream permissions

Both datasets are available under open licences that allow people to reuse, modify, and share the information. This means others can use the data and the results from my project, provided they follow the conditions of the original licences. Anyone reusing my project must give credit to Statistics Canada and the Government of Canada using the required attribution statements. They must also make sure their use does not suggest that either organization endorses their work. I will keep the original sources and their licence information clearly identified in my project.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 4: Consent and identifiability

Neither dataset contains information about individual people. The grocery dataset reports average food prices by province and month, while the minimum wage dataset reports wage rates. Datasets contains economic information rather than personal records, names, or other identifying details.

**Consent.** I did not collect any information directly from participants or conduct surveys or interviews. Both datasets were collected and published by government organizations for public use.

**Identifiability.** The datasets do not identify individuals. The smallest level of information used in my analysis is based on a province, product, and month for grocery prices, or a jurisdiction and effective date for minimum wages. Since the data is reported at these levels rather than for individual people, there is no risk of identifying someone through my analysis.

**How sensitive data will be used.** Neither dataset contains sensitive personal information. I will not be collecting or publishing names, addresses, financial records, or other personal details. My analysis will focus on provincial averages and minimum wage rates, so no additional steps to hide individual identities are needed.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 5: Exclusions and harms

## 5.1: Excluded data from the audit

In the grocery datasets, the first row after importing the CSV contains the word "Dollars" to describe the units of measurement rather than an actual grocery product. I will remove this row because it is not useful for the analysis. I will also exclude any columns or rows that are not needed for comparing grocery prices over time. For the minimum wage dataset, I will focus on provincial minimum wage rates and exclude federal rates.

One limitation is that the grocery price data only goes back to September 2019, so I cannot include the years before that in my comparison.

## 5.2: Who could be harmed

Someone could misuse my results to suggest that minimum-wage workers can easily afford groceries. However, my project only looks at selected food prices and does not include other costs like rent, transportation, and bills. This could give people the wrong idea about how affordable life really is for minimum-wage workers. I will make these limitations clear when presenting my results.

## 5.3: Unreleased working data

I do not have any working data that needs to be kept private. Both datasets are publicly available and contain grocery prices and minimum wage information, not personal details. I am comfortable sharing the original data, cleaned datasets, and code so others can review and reproduce my work.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 6: Data Stewardship

**Where it lives.** The project files will be stored in my GitHub repository. This includes the original CSV files, cleaned datasets, R Markdown document, and analysis code.

**Who maintains it.** I will maintain the project during the course. I do not currently plan to update it regularly after the course ends though.

**Formats and dependencies.** The data is saved in CSV files, and my project is written in R Markdown. I use packages like `tidyverse` and `knitr`. In the future, updates to these packages/changes to the data links might affect my project.

**Lifespan.** The project will remain useful as a historical comparison of grocery prices and minimum wages from 2019 to 2026. However, it may become less useful for understanding current affordability as prices and wages change.
